title: Read the Rails/Kafka app one file at a time
outcome: Run and explain the complete multi-file path from HTTP completion to a repeat-safe reporting projection.
benefits: Turns abstract Kafka guarantees into inspectable files and failure drills.
drawbacks: A deliberately small local topology has documented production limits.
version: Kafka 4.1 KRaft · lab Ruby 3.3 / Rails 7.2 · legacy Rails adaptation notes
cue: One file, one boundary, one observable state.

trace.title: HTTP service
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

The local lab uses fresh support-ticket code. It borrows broad production patterns—service objects, transactions, workers, and projections—without copying private application code or data.

It uses Ruby 3.3/Rails 7.2 with a pinned Kafka client; that is separate from the Ruby 2.7/Rails 4.2 work baseline.

Read in this order: routes/controller, CompleteTicket service, migrations/models, envelope builder, Kafka producer adapter, outbox dispatcher, reporting projector, consumer loop, and tests. Each file owns one boundary.

Infrastructure/config files explain how the processes find one another.

Run the smoke script and failure drills with synthetic data. Do not merely watch logs scroll.

Predict the ticket, outbox, topic, inbox, and projection state at each stop point. The app contains no real email, analytics, or cloud credentials.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Create one synthetic ticket. Complete it twice: the business transition should create one logical completion event.

Wait for reporting: one inbox/effect appears. Re-publish the saved envelope: Kafka can contain another record with the same event_id, while the local projection effect remains one.

Stop the dispatcher before completion, then restart it. Saved intent should still be found.

Stop the consumer, publish, then restart it. Retained history and group progress should let it catch up within retention.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: The lab is intentionally one broker and one serial dispatcher. It does not prove multi-zone HA, high-throughput ordering under several dispatchers, production auth, or every legacy-fork behavior.
